claim: Transcriptomic profiling of ductal cells after beta cell destruction in adult zebrafish revealed that 1866 genes are upregulated and 1515 genes downregulated (padj < 0.05).
source: Differential gene expression analysis revealed that 1866 genes are upregulated and 1515 genes downregulated in the ductal cell of fish treated with MTZ compared to control (padj < 0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental RNA-sequencing data from ductal cells following beta cell ablation, with statistical analysis using DESeq2.

claim: DNA replication and cell cycle are the most enriched pathways among upregulated genes in ductal cells after beta cell ablation.
source: According to Gene Ontology (GO) analysis, the most enriched pathways among the upregulated genes were DNA replication and cell cycle (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Gene Ontology analysis of RNA-sequencing data and is visualized in Figure 1A showing enrichment ratios.

claim: The Notch pathway was enriched in the downregulated genes after beta cell ablation in ductal cells.
source: As expected, the Notch pathway was enriched in the downregulated genes (Ninov et al., 2013; Ninov et al., 2012; Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data analysis and is consistent with previous studies cited (Ninov et al., 2013; Ninov et al., 2012).

claim: Several components of the calcineurin signaling pathway including nfatc3b, ppp3ccb, itpr2, and calm3b are associated with the cellular senescence signature in ductal cells after beta cell ablation.
source: We found among them several components of the CaN signaling pathway such as nfatc3b, ppp3ccb (the catalytic subunit of CaN), itpr2, and calm3b (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is based on transcriptomic data showing these genes are part of the cellular senescence signature.

claim: Calcineurin is a highly conserved calcium/calmodulin-dependent Ser/Thr phosphatase involved in numerous biological processes including fin regeneration and beta cell function.
source: CaN is a highly conserved calcium/calmodulin-dependent Ser/Thr phosphatase, involved in numerous biological process including fin regeneration and beta cell function (Tornini, 2016; McMillan et al., 2018; Cao et al., 2021; Kujawski et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations describing calcineurin's biochemical nature and biological roles.

claim: Duct-associated beta cells started to be detected in non-ablated larvae between 7 and 10 days post treatment (dpt).
source: Duct-associated beta cells started to be detected in non-ablated larvae between 7 and 10 dpt (Figure 1F)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data from Tg(ins:NTR-P2A-mCherry); Tg(nkx6.1:GFP) larvae shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In ablated larvae, the increase in beta cell number became more pronounced from 10 dpt onwards, indicating faster endocrine differentiation.
source: In ablated larvae, the increase became more pronounced from 10 dpt onwards (Figure 1F, G), indicating faster endocrine differentiation.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data and microscopy images showing increased beta cell formation in ablated conditions.

claim: Acute beta cell ablation in larvae rapidly activates ductal cell proliferation.
source: This result shows that acute beta cell ablation in larvae rapidly activates ductal cell proliferation, as previously reported in adult zebrafish.
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU incorporation assay data showing increased proportion of GFP+ ductal cells EdU+ in ablated larvae (Figure 1I, J).

claim: Cyclosporin A (CsA) treatment enhanced beta cell formation at 10 dpt after beta cell ablation in larvae.
source: CsA-enhanced beta cell formation at 10 dpt (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from Tg(ins:NTR-P2A-mCherry); Tg(nkx6.1:GFP) larvae treated with CsA.

claim: The effect of CsA on beta cell regeneration appears to be transient since no discernible difference was observed between control and CsA-treated larvae at 14 dpt.
source: However, this effect appears to be transient since no discernible difference was observed between the control and CsA-treated larvae in regeneration at the latest time point (14 dpt), suggesting an acceleration of the regenerative response (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course data showing convergence of beta cell numbers at 14 dpt.

claim: CsA did not affect beta cell differentiation in non-ablated larvae, indicating that CsA only acts in a regenerative context.
source: Interestingly, CsA did not affect beta cell differentiation in non-ablated larvae, indicating that CsA only acts in a regenerative context (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of beta cell numbers in non-ablated larvae with and without CsA treatment.

claim: CsA increased the number of regenerated beta cells in the principal islet.
source: Of note, CsA increased as well the number of regenerated beta cells in the principal islet (Figure 2—figure supplement 1(2) and (3)).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data from the principal islet shown in supplementary figures.

claim: CsA did not affect bi-hormonal cell formation.
source: However, CsA did not affect bi-hormonal cell formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1(4)), suggesting that the additional cells in the principal islet could also originate from the ducts.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of sst1.1+/mCherry+ bi-hormonal cells showing no difference with CsA treatment.

claim: CsA induced an increase of neurod1+ cells from 4 dpt that was still detectable at least until 10 dpt.
source: We first assessed generation of GFP cells at different time points (Figure 2—figure supplement 1(5)) and showed that CsA induced an increase of neurod1+ cells from 4 dpt. The increase was still detectable at least until 10 dpt (Figure 2E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1(6)).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course quantification of neurod1+ cells in Tg(neurod1:GFP) larvae.

claim: CsA did not affect the neurod1+ cell proliferation rate.
source: We observed that CsA did not affect the neurod1+ cell proliferation rate, which is very low at these stages (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU incorporation assay in neurod1+ cells showing no change in proliferation with CsA.

claim: The effect of CsA on beta cell formation cannot be explained by endocrine cell proliferation but rather by neogenesis from progenitors.
source: As a consequence, the effect of CsA cannot be explained by endocrine cell proliferation but rather by neogenesis from progenitors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that CsA increases neurod1+ cells without affecting their proliferation rate.

claim: CsA did not affect alpha nor delta1.1 cells neogenesis in response to beta cell ablation.
source: Interestingly, CsA did not affect alpha nor delta1.1 cells neogenesis in response to beta cell ablation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1(7), (8)).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence quantification of alpha and delta cells with CsA treatment.

claim: CsA affects specifically the beta cells and their endocrine progenitors.
source: Overall, these experiments showed that CsA affects specifically the beta cells and their endocrine progenitors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that CsA affects beta cells and neurod1+ cells but not alpha or delta cells.

claim: Overexpression of constitutively active calcineurin (CaNCA) after beta cell ablation impaired the regenerative response at 14 dpt.
source: The overexpression of CaNCA after ablation impaired the regenerative response at 14 dpt (Figure 3B, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of beta cells in Tg(hsp70:GFP-P2A-ppp3ccCA) larvae with heat-shock induced CaNCA expression.

claim: Continuous and specific overexpression of CaNCA in the ducts suppressed the regenerative response.
source: Similar results were obtained with Tg(UAS:GFP-P2A-ppp3ccCA); Tg(cftr:gal4) (Liu et al., 2018); Tg(ins:NTR-P2A-mCherry) larvae in which CaNCA is continuously and specifically overexpressed in the ducts within the pancreas (Figure 3D, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by beta cell quantification in larvae with duct-specific CaNCA overexpression using the cftr:gal4 driver.

claim: The structure of the ducts was similar in CaNCA overexpressing larvae compared to controls, suggesting that the suppression of the regenerative response was not due to morphogenetic defects during ductal growth.
source: Importantly, the structure of the ducts was similar in CaNCA overexpressing larvae compared to Tg(nkx6.1:GFP) controls (Figure 3D), suggesting that the suppression of the regenerative response in CaNCA-overexpressing larvae was not due to morphogenetic defects during ductal growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy images showing normal ductal structure in CaNCA overexpressing larvae.

claim: Calcineurin acts directly in the ducts to decrease beta cell regeneration while it is not necessary for normal beta cell differentiation.
source: This result shows that CaN acts directly in the ducts to decrease beta cell regeneration while it is not necessary for normal beta cell differentiation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that duct-specific CaNCA overexpression inhibits regeneration without affecting normal development.

claim: Notch inhibition with LY411575 progressively increased the number of beta cells as the concentration increased.
source: As expected, the number of beta cells progressively rose as the concentration of the Notch inhibitor increased (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data showing increased beta cell formation with increasing LY411575 concentrations.

claim: Combined treatment with CsA and LY411575 fostered the differentiation of beta cells between 1 and 10 µM LY411575 but did not result in further increase at 15 µM LY411575.
source: Combined treatment with CsA fostered the differentiation of beta cells between 1 and 10 µM LY411575 but did not result in further increase at 15 µM LY411575 (Figure 4B), suggesting that CaN is important within a permissive window of Notch activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data showing synergistic effects of CsA and LY411575 at intermediate concentrations.

claim: Combined treatment of LY411575 (5 µM) and FK506 resulted in the same synergistic increase of beta cell differentiation, confirming that the effect is due to calcineurin inhibition.
source: It is worth noting that combined treatment of LY411575 (5 µM) and another CaN inhibitor, FK506, resulted in the same synergistic increase of beta cell differentiation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1(1), (2)), confirming that the effect is well due to CaN inhibition.
evidence: The claim is supported by data using a second calcineurin inhibitor (FK506) showing similar effects to CsA.

claim: The combined effect of Notch and calcineurin inhibition is transient as it is not observed at 7 dpf anymore.
source: The combined effect of Notch and CaN inhibition is transient as it is not observed at 7 dpf anymore (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course data showing convergence of beta cell numbers by 7 dpf.

claim: Calcineurin inhibition accelerates beta cell neogenesis induced by Notch repression.
source: Therefore, as observed in regenerative conditions (Figure 2B), CaN inhibition accelerates beta cell neogenesis induced by Notch repression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the transient increase in beta cell formation with combined CsA and Notch inhibition.

claim: CaNCA overexpression resulted in lowered beta cell formation induced by Notch inhibition, revealing that calcineurin activation counterbalanced the effects of Notch inhibition.
source: CaNCA overexpression resulted in a lowered beta cell formation induced by Notch inhibition Figure 4—figure supplement 1(4), revealing that CaN activation counterbalanced the effects of Notch inhibition.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing reduced beta cell formation when CaNCA is overexpressed during Notch inhibition.

claim: CHIR99021 rescued the effect of CsA on beta cell neogenesis, suggesting that calcineurin inhibition increases beta cell neogenesis at least partially by the regulation of NFAT.
source: We found that CHIR99021 rescued the effect of CsA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1(5)), suggesting that CaN inhibition increases beta cell neogenesis at least partially by the regulation of NFAT.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that NFAT activation with CHIR99021 reverses the effects of CsA.

claim: Calcineurin and Notch pathways act on a common pool of ductal progenitors to govern beta cell neogenesis.
source: Moreover, it suggests that both CaN and Notch pathways act on a common pool of ductal progenitors to govern beta cell neogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the synergistic effects of CaN and Notch inhibition on beta cell formation.

claim: Notch inhibition increased the proportion of proliferating EdU+ GFP+ ductal cells at 4 dpf while the number of GFP+ ductal cells remained constant.
source: As expected, Notch inhibition increased the proportion of proliferating EdU+ GFP+ ductal cells at 4 dpf (Figure 5B, C) while the number of GFP+ ductal cells remained constant (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU incorporation assay data showing increased proliferation without change in total ductal cell number.

claim: The amount of ductal progenitors decreased 2 days later (at 6 dpf), which is concomitant with the increase of beta cell differentiation.
source: Furthermore, the amount of ductal progenitors decreased 2 days later (at 6 dpf) (Figure 5D), which is concomitant with the increase of beta cell differentiation (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data showing reduced ductal cell numbers at 6 dpf correlating with increased beta cell formation.

claim: Combined inhibition with CsA and LY411575 further increased the proportion of proliferating ductal cells, while CaN inhibition alone had no effect.
source: Interestingly, the combined inhibition with CsA further increased these proportions, while CaN inhibition alone had no effect (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU incorporation data showing synergistic effects of CsA and LY411575 on ductal cell proliferation.

claim: Beta cells EdU+ were detected at 6 dpf, indicating that these cells originate from the proliferation of ductal progenitors.
source: Of note, we detected beta cells EdU+ at 6 dpf (Figure 5—figure supplement 1(2)), underlying that these cells originate from the proliferation of ductal progenitors.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy images showing EdU-labeled beta cells, indicating they arose from proliferating progenitors.

claim: After stronger Notch inhibition (15 µM LY411575), the ductal cells are already depleted at 4 dpf as they directly differentiate without entering the cell cycle.
source: In comparison, after stronger Notch inhibition (15 µM), the ductal cells are already depleted at 4 dpf (Figure 5—figure supplement 1(3)), as they directly differentiate without entering the cell cycle (Ninov et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data showing reduced ductal cell numbers at 4 dpf with high-dose Notch inhibition, consistent with previous findings (Ninov et al., 2012).

claim: Calcineurin and Notch pathways act together on the proliferation of the ductal progenitors to prevent their exhaustion.
source: These results show that CaN and Notch pathways act together on the proliferation of the ductal progenitors to prevent their exhaustion.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that combined CaN and Notch inhibition increases proliferation but leads to progenitor depletion.

claim: Calcineurin inhibition enhanced the proliferation of ductal cells in ablated larvae.
source: CaN inhibition enhanced the proliferation of ductal cells in ablated larvae (Figure 5F, G).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU incorporation data in Tg(ins:NTR-P2A-mCherry); Tg(nkx6.1:GFP) larvae after ablation and CsA treatment.

claim: In ablated larvae, CsA increased tp1+ ductal cell proliferation.
source: In ablated-larvae, CsA increased tp1+ ductal cell proliferation (Figure 5H, I).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU incorporation data in Tg(tp1:VenusPest) Notch reporter larvae showing increased proliferation of Notch-responsive cells.

claim: CsA induced a reduction of tp1+ ductal cells in ablated larvae, suggesting an exhaustion of the Notch responsive progenitors.
source: Moreover, CsA induced a reduction of tp1+ ductal cells in ablated larvae (Figure 5H–J), suggesting an exhaustion of the Notch responsive progenitors, in accordance with premature beta cell differentiation we observed (Figures 2B–4D—4).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data showing reduced tp1+ cell numbers with CsA treatment in ablated larvae.

claim: CsA does not affect tp1+ cells in non-ablated larvae showing that calcineurin inhibition did not directly affect Notch signaling.
source: Lastly, CsA does not affect tp1+ cells in non-ablated larvae showing that CaN inhibition did not directly affect Notch signaling (Figure 5J).
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing no change in tp1+ cell numbers with CsA in non-ablated conditions.

claim: Calcineurin fine tunes the balance between proliferation of the progenitors and their differentiation to prevent their exhaustion during beta cell regeneration.
source: Those results suggest that CaN fine tunes the balance between proliferation of the progenitors and their differentiation to prevent their exhaustion during beta cell regeneration.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that CaN inhibition increases both proliferation and differentiation, leading to progenitor depletion.

claim: In 2-month-old juvenile zebrafish, CsA increased the number of small islets at 7 dpt in ablated juveniles.
source: At 7 dpt, CsA increased the number of small islets in ablated juveniles (Figure 6A, B) showing that CaN inhibition enhances beta cell regeneration in juvenile zebrafish, as in larvae.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of small islets in 2-month-old Tg(ins:NTR-P2A-mCherry); Tg(nkx6.1:GFP) fish.

claim: The increase in small islets with CsA treatment is transient as it is not observed anymore at 10 dpt in juvenile zebrafish.
source: The increase number of small islets is indeed transient as it not observe anymore at 10 dpt (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course data showing convergence of small islet numbers by 10 dpt in juveniles.

claim: Overexpression of CaNCA using either Tg(hsp70:GFP-P2A-ppp3ccCA) or Tg(cftr:gal4); Tg(UAS:GFP-P2A-ppp3ccCA) led to increased glycemia at both 7 and 10 dpt in adult zebrafish.
source: Overexpression of CaNCA using either Tg(hsp70:GFP-P2A-ppp3ccCA) or Tg(cftr:gal4); Tg(UAS:GFP-P2A-ppp3ccCA), led to an increased glycemia at both 7 and 10 dpt (Figure 6D, E), before recovery at 14 dpt (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by glycemia measurements in adult zebrafish with CaNCA overexpression.

claim: Overexpression of calcineurin delayed glycemia recovery induced by beta cell regeneration in adult zebrafish.
source: This indicates that the overexpression of CaN delayed glycemia recovery induced by beta cell regeneration.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that CaNCA overexpression leads to prolonged hyperglycemia after beta cell ablation.

claim: Calcineurin inhibition did not further improve glycemia in adult zebrafish probably because the glycemia was already low at 7 dpt compared to non-ablated control.
source: However, CaN inhibition did not seem to further improve the glycemia (Figure 6D, E) probably because the glycemia was already low at 7 dpt (77 mg/dl on average) compared to non-ablated control (50 mg/dl on average) (Figure 6D, E).
evidence: The claim is inferred from glycemia measurements showing limited room for improvement with CsA treatment.

claim: In adult zebrafish, calcineurin regulation is necessary to enable beta cell regeneration and for proper recovery of the glycemia after beta cell loss.
source: Altogether, these results show that in adult zebrafish also, CaN regulation is necessary to enable beta cell regeneration and for proper recovery of the glycemia after beta cell loss.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined observations of CaNCA overexpression delaying glycemia recovery and CsA enhancing regeneration.

claim: Beta cell destruction is largely irreversible in humans and mammals, making diabetes incurable nowadays.
source: Beta cell destruction is largely irreversible in human and in mammals, making the disease incurable nowadays.
evidence: The claim reflects established scientific consensus about the limited regenerative capacity of human beta cells.

claim: New beta cells can arise from the replication of remaining beta cells in diabetic mice models.
source: For example, new beta cells can arise from the replication of remaining beta cells (Dor et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dor et al., 2004.

claim: Differentiated endocrine cells such as alpha cells and delta cells can reprogram and convert into insulin-producing cells in an age-dependent process.
source: Actually, differentiated endocrine cells such as alpha cells (Thorel, 2010) and delta cells (Chera, 2014) can reprogram and convert into insulin-producing cells, a process that is age dependent.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Thorel, 2010 and Chera, 2014.

claim: Expression of the pro-endocrine marker Neurog3 was detected in the ducts in different mouse models of pancreas regeneration.
source: However, expression of the pro-endocrine marker Neurog3 was detected in the ducts in different mouse models of pancreas regeneration (Xu et al., 2008; Kopp et al., 2011; Courtney et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations describing Neurog3 expression in ductal cells during regeneration.

claim: A rare population of ductal cells expressing Neurog3 has been reported to contribute to beta cell neogenesis during diabetes.
source: In addition, a rare population of ductal cells expressing Neurog3 has been reported to contribute to beta cell neogenesis during diabetes (Gribben et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gribben et al., 2021.

claim: A sub-population of human ductal cells are able to give rise to all the pancreatic cell types, including beta cells, following implantation in mice.
source: A recent study of single-cell RNA sequencing reveal a sub-population of human ductal cells which are able to give rise to all the pancreatic cell types, including beta cells, following implantation in mice (Qadir et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Qadir et al., 2020 describing single-cell RNA sequencing results.

claim: Mammalian pancreatic ducts possess the intrinsic capacity to (re)generate beta cells even though this process is poorly efficient and slow, especially in adults.
source: Altogether, these findings suggest that mammalian pancreatic ducts possess the intrinsic capacity to (re)generate beta cells even though this process is poorly efficient and slow, especially in adults.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple cited studies showing limited but present regenerative capacity in mammalian ducts.

claim: Zebrafish possess remarkable capacity of regeneration, independently of age.
source: In contrast to mammals, zebrafish possess remarkable capacity of regeneration, independently of its age (Moss et al., 2009; Poss et al., 2002; Choi et al., 2014; Goldshmit et al., 2012; Kroehne et al., 2011; Gemberling et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations describing zebrafish regenerative capacity.

claim: Several studies based on regenerative mechanisms identified in zebrafish succeeded in improving regeneration in mammals.
source: Based on regenerative mechanisms identified in zebrafish, several studies succeed to improve regeneration in mammals, underlying the possibility of translation from zebrafish to mammals (Papadimitriou et al., 2018; Mashkaryan et al., 2020; Ko et al., 2016; Goldshmit et al., 2015; Fausett et al., 2008; Massoz et al., 2021, for review).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations showing successful translation of zebrafish findings to mammalian systems.

claim: Beta cell destruction is complete within 3 days following metronidazole treatment in adult Tg(ins:NTR-mCherry) fish, which correlates with a peak of hyperglycemia.
source: When NTR is expressed under the control of the insulin (ins) promoter (Tg(ins:NTR-mCherry); Pisharath et al., 2007), beta cell destruction is complete within 3 days following the treatment in adult fish, which correlate with a peak of hyperglycemia (Delaspre et al., 2015; Ghaye et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Delaspre et al., 2015 and Ghaye et al., 2015 describing the ablation kinetics.

claim: The regeneration of beta cells upon ablation is spontaneous and fast and the glycemia is normalized within 2 weeks in zebrafish.
source: The regeneration of beta cells upon ablation is spontaneous and fast and the glycemia is normalized within 2 weeks (Choi et al., 2014; Ye et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Choi et al., 2014 and Ye et al., 2015.

claim: New beta cells can arise through proliferation of surviving beta cells in zebrafish.
source: Similar to mice, new beta cells can arise through proliferation of surviving beta cells (Andersson, 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Andersson, 2012.

claim: Alpha cells and delta cells contribute to beta cell regeneration in zebrafish.
source: as well as through the contribution of alpha cells (Ye et al., 2015; Helker et al., 2019) and delta cells (Pardo, 2022; Singh et al., 2022), underscoring the overall conservation of these processes from zebrafish to mammals.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations describing alpha-to-beta and delta-to-beta cell conversion.

claim: The presence of pancreatic progenitors in the ducts is well established in both larval and adult zebrafish.
source: Nevertheless, unlike mammals, the presence of pancreatic progenitors in the ducts is well established in both larval (Ninov et al., 2013) and adult zebrafish (Delaspre et al., 2015; Ghaye et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating ductal progenitors in zebrafish.

claim: Lineage tracing experiments showed that ductal cells and centroacinar cells (CACs) give rise to new beta cells in zebrafish.
source: Lineage tracing experiments pointed out that ductal cells and centroacinar cells (CACs) give rise to new beta cells (Delaspre et al., 2015; Ninov et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to lineage tracing studies.

claim: In adults, duct-derived beta cells start to be detected between 7 and 10 days following beta cell ablation.
source: In adults, duct-derived beta cells start to be detected between 7 and 10 days following beta cell ablation (Delaspre et al., 2015; Ghaye et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies describing the timing of duct-derived beta cell appearance.

claim: Notch signaling is a key player regulating the differentiation of duct-associated progenitors into endocrine cells.
source: Notch signaling is a key player regulating the differentiation of duct-associated progenitors into endocrine cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by the subsequent discussion of Notch's role and citations.

claim: Larval duct cells and adult CACs display strong Notch activity.
source: Larval duct cells as well as adult CACs display strong Notch activity (Delaspre et al., 2015; Parsons et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies showing Notch activity in ductal cells.

claim: Notch signaling has a central role in beta cell genesis during both development and regeneration by repressing endocrine differentiation.
source: This signaling pathway has a central role in beta cell genesis during both development (Ninov et al., 2012) and regeneration (Ninov et al., 2013) by repressing endocrine differentiation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies describing Notch's role in development and regeneration.

claim: Different levels of Notch activity determine the behavior of pancreatic progenitors in zebrafish: high level maintains quiescence, moderate level induces cell cycle entry and proliferation, and low level drives endocrine differentiation.
source: In zebrafish, different levels of Notch activity determine the behavior of the pancreatic progenitors. While a high level of Notch activity maintains cells in quiescence, a moderate level induces the entry in the cell cycle and proliferation whereas a low level drives endocrine differentiation of the progenitor cells (Ninov et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ninov et al., 2012 describing Notch activity levels and progenitor behavior.

claim: A steep decrease of Notch activity pushes progenitors to differentiate prematurely, bypassing the amplification step and leading to their depletion.
source: A steep decrease of Notch activity pushes the progenitors to differentiate prematurely, bypassing the amplification step and leading to their depletion (Ninov et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ninov et al., 2012.

claim: Repression of Notch signaling by mTor, activated by glucose and nutrients, promotes beta cell formation and regeneration from ductal progenitors.
source: Repression of the Notch signaling by mTor, activated by glucose and nutrients, hence promotes beta cell formation and regeneration from ductal progenitors (Ninov et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ninov et al., 2013 describing mTor-Notch interactions.

claim: In the regenerating fin, low calcineurin activity is found in the proximal region of the blastema characterized by high rate of proliferation and regeneration, and its activity increases distally where lower proliferation is observed.
source: In the regenerating fin, low CaN activity is found in the proximal region of the blastema characterized by a high rate of proliferation and regeneration and its activity increases distally where lower proliferation is observed (Tornini, 2016; Cao et al., 2021; Kujawski et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations describing calcineurin activity patterns in fin regeneration.

claim: Calcineurin was suggested to control blastemal cell progeny divisions during fin regeneration.
source: It was suggested that CaN control blastemal cell progeny divisions (Tornini, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tornini, 2016.

claim: Organ transplant patients treated with Cyclosporin A as immunosuppressive drug present an increased risk of skin cancer, notably due to keratinocyte senescence inhibition.
source: In human, the importance of CaN in proliferation is also highlighted in organ transplanted patients. When patients are treated with Cyclosporin A (i.e. the CaN inhibitor we used in this study) as immunosuppressive drug they indeed present an increased risk of skin cancer, notably due to keratinocyte senescence inhibition (Wu, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wu, 2010 describing clinical observations in transplant patients.

claim: In differentiating keratinocytes, calcineurin cooperates with Notch signaling to regulate p21/cdkn1a, cell cycle withdrawal and differentiation.
source: In differentiating keratinocytes, CaN cooperates with Notch signaling to regulate p21/cdkn1a (which is upregulated in the ducts at 3 dpt), cell cycle withdrawal and differentiation (Mammucari et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mammucari et al., 2005 describing CaN-Notch cooperation in keratinocytes.

claim: Three division modes of pancreatic progenitors exist during embryonic development in mice: symmetric self-renewing resulting in two progenitor cells, asymmetric resulting in a progenitor and an endocrine cell, and symmetric differentiative resulting in two differentiated cells.
source: More precisely, a previous study in mice uncover the existence of three division modes of the pancreatic progenitors during embryonic development, that is symmetric self-renewing resulting in two progenitors cells; asymmetric resulting in a progenitor and a endocrine cell and symmetric differentiative resulting in two differentiated cells (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2015 describing division modes in mouse pancreatic progenitors.

claim: The type of division in pancreatic progenitors is defined by the timing of induction of endocrine program by NEUROG3.
source: The authors actually show that the type of division is defined by the timing of induction of endocrine program by NEUROG3 (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2015.

claim: NEUROG3 expression is regulated by Notch signaling.
source: Interestingly, NEUROG3 seems to be the link between proliferation and differentiation, and its expression is regulated by Notch signaling (Krentz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Krentz et al., 2017.

claim: In zebrafish, endocrine differentiation is not induced by Neurog3 but by Ascl1b and Neurod1.
source: In zebrafish, endocrine differentiation is not induced by Neurog3 but by Ascl1b and Neurod1 (Flasse et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Flasse et al., 2013 describing zebrafish endocrine differentiation factors.

claim: In stem cells and neuronal and hematopoietic progenitors, premature differentiation results from a switch in the mode of cellular division, from symmetric amplifying division to asymmetric differentiating division.
source: In stem cells and neuronal and hematopoietic progenitors, premature differentiation results from a switch in the mode of cellular division, from symmetric amplifying division to asymmetric differentiating division (Huttner and Kosodo, 2005; Ho and Wagner, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations describing division mode switches in various progenitor types.

claim: Notch determines the choice between symmetric and asymmetric types of divisions.
source: Notch determines the choice between both types of divisions (Bultje et al., 2009; Guo et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies showing Notch's role in determining division modes.

claim: Calcineurin is known to be implicated in cellular senescence.
source: CaN is known to be implicated in cellular senescence (Wu, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wu, 2010.

claim: DNA repair and cellular senescence appear to be required in both developmental and regenerative processes.
source: Usually thought as negative regulators of development and cellular growth, DNA repair (Sousounis et al., 2020) and cellular senescence (Da Silva‐Álvarez et al., 2020) appear to be required in both developmental and regenerative processes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent studies showing positive roles of DNA repair and senescence.

claim: Some studies report an increase of proliferation of some ductal cell population in diabetic patients.
source: Some studies report an increase of proliferation of some ductal cell population in diabetic patients (Qadir et al., 2020; Moin et al., 2017), implying a regenerative response.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies in diabetic patients.

claim: Ductal cells in diabetic patients cannot efficiently reform the beta cell mass, suggesting a dormant mechanism of regeneration.
source: However, these ductal cells cannot efficiently reform the beta cell mass, suggesting a dormant mechanism of regeneration.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that despite increased proliferation, beta cell mass is not restored in diabetic patients.

claim: Calcineurin is important for beta cell function.
source: However, as CaN is also important for beta cell function, this approach would require to be transient to induce neogenesis.
evidence: The claim reflects established knowledge about calcineurin's role in beta cell function.

claim: The transcriptomic data were generated from ductal cells at 3 days post ablation treatment, before beta cell neogenesis.
source: To capture the early events triggered by the destruction of beta cells, we generated the transcriptome of the ducts 3 days post ablation treatment (dpt), that is before beta cell neogenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design for the transcriptomic study.

claim: Calcineurin genes (ppp3cca/b) and nfatc3b are expressed at lower levels in the ducts at basal state but their expression is induced in response to beta cell destruction.
source: CaN genes (ppp3cca/b) as well as nfatc3b are express at lower levels in the ducts at basal state but their expression is induced in response to beta cell destruction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1(3)).
evidence: The claim is supported by expression data from ductal cells in non-ablated and ablated conditions.

claim: Calcineurin (ppp3ccb and ppp3cca) and NFATc3 (nfatc3a and nfatc3b) are mainly expressed in endocrine cells.
source: Previous RNAseq data performed in our laboratory indicate that CaN (ppp3cca/b) and NFATc3 (nfatc3a/b) are mainly express in endocrine cells (Tarifeño-Saldivia et al., 2017; Figure 1—figure supplement 1(2)), which is in accordance with the role of CaN/NFAT signaling in beta cells (Heit et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by previous RNA-sequencing data from the authors' laboratory and is consistent with known roles of CaN/NFAT in beta cells.
